title: Aquinas: an act can be praiseworthy and meritorious though the will be determined to one thing
source_text: XVIII. Hinc est quod docet opus quoddam esse posse laude, vel vituperio dignum, meritorium, vel demeritorium, ex hoc quod est spontaneum non coactum & voluntarium, tametsi voluntas illius respectu sit ad unum determinata. Nam in tertium sententiarum scribens, [marg.: Dist. 12. q. 2. art. 1. ad 3.] Impotentia coactionis, inquit, quae opponitur voluntario, tollit rationem meriti & demeriti, non impotentia quae est ex perfectione in bonitate, vel malitia, quia hoc voluntarium non tollit, sed ponit voluntatem confirmatam ad unum. Et in eodem libro, ut explicaret quomodo Christus mereri potuerit per liberum arbitrium determinatum ad unum numero, scilicet ad diligendum Deum: [marg.: Dist. 18. art. 2. ad 5.] Dicendum, inquit, quod etiamsi esset determinatum ad unum numero sicut ad diligendum Deum, quod non facere non potest: tamen ex hoc, non amittit libertatem, aut rationem laudis, sive meriti, quia in illud non coacte, sed sponte tendit, & ita est actus sui Dominus.
pass_a_gloss: Hence it is that he teaches that some work can be worthy of praise, or blame, meritorious, or demeritorious, from this that it is spontaneous, not compelled, and voluntary, although the will be determined to one thing in respect of it. For writing on the third of the sentences, [marg.: Dist. 12. q. 2. art. 1. ad 3.] The impotence of compulsion, he says, which is opposed to the voluntary, takes away the character of merit and demerit, not the impotence which is from perfection in goodness, or malice, because this does not take away the voluntary, but posits the will confirmed to one thing. And in the same book, to explain how Christ could merit through free choice determined to one thing in number, namely to loving God: [marg.: Dist. 18. art. 2. ad 5.] It must be said, he says, that even if it were determined to one thing in number, as to loving God, which it cannot not do: yet from this, it does not lose liberty, or the character of praise, or merit, because it tends into that not compelled, but spontaneously, and so is master of its act.
pass_b_english: So he teaches that a deed may deserve praise or blame, merit or demerit, simply because it is spontaneous, voluntary, and not forced, even though the will is fixed on that one thing.

On the third book of the Sentences (margin: dist. 12, q. 2, art. 1, ad 3) he writes: 'The inability that comes from compulsion, which is the opposite of the voluntary, removes merit and demerit. Not so the inability that comes from perfection in good or in evil. That does not remove the voluntary; it presupposes a will confirmed in one direction.'

In the same book (margin: dist. 18, art. 2, ad 5) he explains how Christ could merit by a free choice fixed on one single act, namely the love of God: 'Even if it were fixed on one single act, such as loving God, which it cannot fail to do, it does not on that account lose its freedom or its claim to praise or merit. It goes toward that act spontaneously and not under force, and so remains in command of its act.'

lemmas.gloss: determined to one thing in number

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
